art.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quieter Monday for art news, but there are two lectures at the Musée de Grenoble, a few local pointers, and some good things to look at or listen to from further afield.

Let me start in Grenoble. The Friends of the Museum have two free talks this week. The first is today, Monday the second of November, at half past two in the afternoon. It looks closely at a work by Le Caire, "La Victorieuse", also known as "La Martiale". It's a chance to spend time with one piece from the museum's own collection, if your afternoon allows. The second is on Wednesday the fourth, at six thirty in the evening, on the Book of Revelation, read as visions, terror and consolation. As a literature teacher, you may find that one especially rewarding, since it's about how a sacred text, full of strange and violent imagery, has gone on inspiring painters and image-makers. A word of caution if you plan to visit: the museum has announced that several rooms are temporarily closed this autumn under the heading "Un musée en mouvement". The notice gives no dates or room details, so it's worth checking before you go.

Staying in the city, Le Pèlerin has a feature on the Tour Perret, describing it as a balcony on the Alps. It's a nice reminder of how Grenoble's architecture and its mountains are bound together.

A little further out, there are three regional pointers. Le Dauphiné Libéré reports that the Y'a tout ça festival in Lans-en-Vercors is being extended into an exhibition, which is close to home for you in the Belledonne and Vercors area. The same paper mentions the autumn exhibition of the Couleurs et volumes group in Saillans, in the Drôme, though the excerpt gives no dates. And in the Isère, the Balcons du Dauphiné are celebrating a hundred and forty years since the birth of the singer Ninon Vallin, with a show at Montalieu-Vercieu. That one brings together local life and classical singing, though again no date is given in what I have.

For Lyon, Le Petit Bulletin has a guide to ten exhibitions to see in November in Lyon and the surrounding area. It is titled "L'éloquence des choses muettes", the eloquence of silent things, which is a lovely phrase and suggests a focus on objects. I only have the headline, so I can't tell you what the individual shows are, but it's a good place to begin if you're planning a trip.

Now to the connections between paintings and stories, which I know you enjoy. The National Gallery in London has a video in which the artist Yinka Shonibare explains how Gainsborough's "Mr and Mrs Andrews" inspired his own reinterpretation, "Mr and Mrs Andrews without their Heads". He talks through his thinking, and the questions it raises about class, power and identity. The two works are being shown together for the first time. For a teacher, it's a wonderful example of one artist reading another, almost like a novelist rewriting a classic. The National Gallery has also released a short film on its Murals ReMastered project, which has brought a reimagined version of Van Gogh's "Sunflowers" to a wall at Westgate in Oxford. It's a cheerful example of great paintings stepping out into everyday public places.

On the subject of reinvention, BBC Radio 4's Front Row has a discussion on how fairy tales are being reinvented and subverted for the twenty-first century. It includes Daniel Foxx's satirical book about privileged children. It's very much about story and narrative voice, and I suspect it might spark some ideas for the classroom.

For something more substantial, The Guardian has a long feature on Geoffrey Bardon and the painters of Papunya. It examines the myth surrounding the origins of Western Desert Aboriginal dot painting, and the title quotes a phrase, "a whitewashing of minds". A new biography has prompted the reassessment. It's a serious account of an art movement and of how its history has been told, so one for a quiet moment.

A few shorter reads. Beaux Arts Magazine has a two-minute profile of Simone Fattal, born in 1942, who has worked for fifty years across painting, sculpture and ceramics. It's a concise introduction to her practice. There's also a digital-museum exhibition, "L'Impressionnisme: sur les traces de Claude Monet", which follows the painter's path. The text is thin, but it may interest you given Monet's place in so many literary conversations.

And to finish on something playful, The Guardian has a photo essay on Jimi Halloween in Tokyo, where adults dress up as ordinary people and perform mundane tasks. It's mostly pictures, and a gentle antidote to all the usual ghouls and witches.

That's the round-up for today, Yamuna. I hope your Monday contains something beautiful to look at.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Monday the second of November, and this morning's art briefing begins close to home in Grenoble, then moves out through the Isère and Lyon before taking in a few stories from further afield.

Two lectures at the Musée de Grenoble first, both put on by the Friends of the Museum. The first is today, Monday, at half past two in the afternoon, and it is free. It is devoted to a work by Le Caire, which goes by two names: "La Victorieuse" or "La Martiale". I like that a single piece should have two titles, one suggesting triumph and the other something sterner, more soldierly. A title does a lot of quiet work in how we look at a thing, which is a lesson you will know well from teaching poems. If your day allows it, it is a good chance to spend an hour looking closely at one object in your own city's collection.

The second lecture is on Wednesday, the fourth of November, at half past six in the evening, and it should suit you even better. It is called "L'Apocalypse de Saint Jean. Visions, Terreur … et Consolation", and it reads the Book of Revelation through those three words: visions, terror and consolation. It is one of the strangest and most intensely imagined texts there is, full of beasts, trumpets and seals, and it has fed painters and engravers for centuries. As a teacher of literature, you might enjoy hearing how a written text gets turned into images, and how the same pages can frighten and comfort at once. The evening hour also makes it easy to attend after a day of teaching.

One practical note, if you are planning a visit. The museum has published a notice called "Un musée en mouvement", saying that several rooms are temporarily closed this autumn. The excerpt does not say which rooms or for how long, so it is worth checking before you go, especially if you are hoping for a particular painting. Perhaps the lectures are the safer way in for the moment.

Still in the city, Le Pèlerin has a feature on the Tour Perret, describing it as a balcony on the Alps. It is the kind of landmark that people in Grenoble see every day and perhaps stop noticing, and a piece like this invites you to look up again. Living as you do in Les Adrets, up on Belledonne, you know the view from the other side, looking down over the Grésivaudan towards the city, so it is rather nice to read about a building that looks back at the mountains.

Now a little further out, with three small local items. First, in Lans-en-Vercors, the Y'a tout ça festival is being prolonged into an exhibition, according to Le Dauphiné Libéré. The text is brief, so I can't tell you much about what will be on the walls, but it is a Vercors event not far from you, and the sort of thing that might make a pleasant autumn outing, perhaps with a stop at a market on the way.

Second, Le Dauphiné Libéré also reports on the autumn exhibition of the group Couleurs & volumes in Saillans, in the Drôme. The name suggests painting and sculpture side by side, though I would be guessing beyond that, and the excerpt gives no dates. It is farther afield, so it may be one to keep in mind rather than to plan around.

Third, there is a more musical note from Montalieu-Vercieu, in the Isère. The Balcons du Dauphiné are putting on a show to celebrate a hundred and forty years since the birth of the singer Ninon Vallin, according to the site mesinfos. No date appears in the excerpt, but it joins local life with classical singing, and since you enjoy concerts and classical music, it is worth looking up the details if you fancy an evening out in the Isère.

Heading to Lyon now. Le Petit Bulletin Lyon has published its guide to ten exhibitions to see in November in Lyon and the surrounding area. It is titled "L'éloquence des choses muettes", the eloquence of silent things, which is a lovely phrase and suggests a thread of objects that speak without words. The extract shows only the headline, so I cannot tell you which ten shows are included. Still, the guide is the right place to start if you are thinking of a day trip, and the title alone could make a good prompt for a class: how can an object, or a still life, be eloquent while saying nothing?

Slightly further afield in France, there is a digital-museum exhibition on jds.fr called "L'Impressionnisme: sur les traces de Claude Monet", tracing the painter's path. The text is thin, so I can't describe how it is organised. But Monet is a good bridge between painting and writing, because Impressionism is so much about light, weather and fleeting moments, which is what poetic prose tries to catch too. If you ever want a way to bring painting into a lesson on descriptive writing, a virtual visit like this could be handy for pupils who can't get to a museum.

Next, to a group of stories that connect art with stories and ideas, which I suspect will be the heart of today's briefing for you. The National Gallery in London has a video in which the artist Yinka Shonibare explains how Gainsborough's "Mr and Mrs Andrews" inspired his own reinterpretation, "Mr and Mrs Andrews without their Heads". He talks through the thinking behind his choices, and the piece takes up class, power and identity. The video also notes that the two works are being shown together for the first time. For a literature teacher it is a rich thing: a painting that already tells a story about property, status and who gets to be looked at, and then an artist answering it, as a writer might answer an earlier novel. It would make a fine way into discussing how a later work talks back to an earlier one, which is what so much of the literature you teach does.

That same idea of retelling turns up on the radio. BBC Radio 4's Front Row has a discussion on how fairy tales are being reinvented and subverted for the twenty-first century. It includes Daniel Foxx's satirical book about privileged children. It is a strongly literary conversation, about narrative voice and about what happens when a familiar story is bent to new ends. Fairy tales are such a good laboratory for this, because everyone half knows the originals, so the twists land immediately. If you are looking for material for your première pupils on adaptation and parody, it might be worth a listen.

There is also a longer read in The Guardian, in its art and design section: a feature titled "A whitewashing of minds", about the mania and myth of Geoffrey Bardon and the painting men of Papunya. It examines the story told about the origins of Western Desert Aboriginal dot painting, and a new biography has prompted this reassessment. It is a substantial account of an art movement and its history, and what makes it interesting is the question of how a founding story gets told, and who is placed at the centre of it. That is a question you can ask of novels and histories as easily as of paintings. It is a good piece for a quiet moment with a cup of tea.

For something shorter, Beaux Arts Magazine has a quick profile, "Simone Fattal en 2 minutes". Fattal was born in 1942 and has worked for fifty years across painting, sculpture and ceramics. It is only a short introduction, but a useful one if her name is new to you, and a reminder of how an artist can move between materials over a long career.

And then two lighter notes to end on. The National Gallery has a short film about its Murals ReMastered project, which has brought a reimagined version of Van Gogh's "Sunflowers" to a wall at Westgate Oxford. It's a cheerful idea: a great painting stepping out of the gallery and into a street where people are simply passing by on their way to something else. There is something very pleasing about a painting meeting someone who wasn't looking for it.

The last item is the most offbeat. The Guardian has a photo essay on "Jimi Halloween", an event in Tokyo where adults dress as ordinary people and perform mundane tasks. The name plays on the Japanese word for plain or unassuming, and the idea is a gentle joke against the usual costumes of Halloween. The piece is mostly pictures, with little text, but it is playful and charming, and a nice contrast to all that gore and ghoulishness. Anyone who has read a novel that finds poetry in ordinary life may well smile at the idea of making the ordinary the costume.

So that is the picture for today: a Le Caire lecture this afternoon, the Apocalypse on Wednesday evening, a few Vercors and Isère shows to look up, and an interesting set of stories about how art and writing keep answering each other.

Enjoy the day, Yamuna, and may the light over Belledonne be kind to you.

literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a gentle, language-minded start to November, with new poetry, some strong voices, and a few prize-season murmurs.

Let me begin with poetry, since there is plenty of it. The New York Times has a review of two new collections that lean into the ecstatic, poems that aim for something almost mystical in their effect. Literary Hub, meanwhile, has its roundup of new poetry to read this November, under the lovely title "Glass Skulls, Luminosity, Soup, and Other Miracles". It is led by Malgorzata Lebda's collection Mer de Glace, in Mira Rosenthal's translation. The opening lines quoted are lyrical, and the translator's notes are mentioned as part of the appeal, which I always find a pleasure, being let into the workshop a little. The title will sound familiar to anyone living near the Alps. Also from Literary Hub, there is a short passage called "The Shared Life of Egan and Lucian". It seems to open a longer piece, and the text we have is thin, but it is set on a bay at sunset, around Shep's Island, and the prose is atmospheric. It might be worth a few minutes with a cup of tea.

Now to voices and characters, which I suspect is where you'll linger. Megan Nolan has written an appreciation of Agnes Owens's novel A Working Mother, presented as an ode to working-class Scotland. It is exactly the sort of piece that makes you want to meet a writer from outside the usual literary circles, and hear a world told by someone who belongs to it. On BBC Radio 4, the Bookclub programme has Matt Haig talking about The Midnight Library. You will know the premise: Nora Seed moves through a library of alternative lives. It is a novel driven by its narrator, and the conversation between Haig and his readers should be a warm one to listen to. And The New York Times reviews Annie Proulx Stories, a career-spanning collection of her short fiction. The reviewer notes her dense, thorny prose, and that is rather the point: sentences you have to lean into, and sharp characters who come out of them.

On the more experimental side, The Guardian reviews Tom McCarthy's new novel, The Rhyl Poster. It follows a war-scarred jurist with a painkiller dependency through a hallucinatory crisis, and the paper calls it an avant-garde spy drama. The reviewer finds the riddles frustrating, and the headline asks outright whether they are worth it. So it may be less a recommendation than an invitation to a debate about whether McCarthy's method pays off, and that could make good material for an argument with colleagues. Also in this vein, the New Statesman has an interview with Missouri Williams under the title "Fiction has its own kind of truth". I only have the headline, so I can't tell you what she says, but it is a good theme to carry around for the day, and one that touches almost everything you teach.

Next, a group of pieces that link writing with music, history and the unseen. The New York Times reviews Graeme Lawson's Sound Tracks, which tells a story of human music-making through ancient instruments. It blends music, archaeology and history, so it sits happily between your interests in sound and in the past. Literary Hub has an essay called "The Ghostly and the Real", on how African literature treats the boundary between the living and the dead. Ancestors and spirits appear there as part of lived reality rather than as decoration, which is a wonderful way into a culture from within, the way a good novel can be. And for nonfiction, Literary Hub offers ten titles to read in November, including new work by Hermione Lee and Orlando Swain. One highlighted book is Matt O'Hara's The Flying Death, about poison, plunder and the search for a medicine in the Amazon. That sounds like a thriller dressed as history.

Finally, the prize corner. The Independent has a piece headlined "What it's like to read one hundred and sixty-three books in seven months", about this year's Booker Prize judges. Only the headline is available, so I can't tell you how they describe the experience, though the number alone is rather staggering. News24 has a guide to the titles in the running for this year's Booker Prize, again just a summary headline, but a handy starting point if you want to see which novels are being talked about. And a nice historical footnote from Literary Hub's "This Week in Literary History": on the fifth of November, nineteen thirty, Sinclair Lewis received the Nobel Prize in Literature, honoured for his vivid description and wit. It is a short note, but a pleasing reminder of how writers are remembered, and by which of their qualities.

If I had to choose a starting point, I'd go for the poetry roundup and the Agnes Owens piece, one for the music of language and the other for the sound of a voice. I hope your day brings a good page or two, and a quiet moment with the mountains in view.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quiet, thoughtful stretch in the reading world this Monday, with a good deal of poetry, some richly voiced fiction, and a few pieces that link books to music, spirits and history.

Let me begin with poetry, since there is plenty of it, and since it's the part of this briefing most likely to be beautiful as language. The New York Times has a review of two new poetry collections that, it says, lean into the ecstatic. That means poems reaching for a heightened, almost mystical effect, where the language is meant to lift the reader out of ordinary attention. I can't tell you more about the individual poets from what I have, but the angle is appealing: poetry that doesn't hold back, that is happy to be rapturous rather than ironic.

Literary Hub, meanwhile, has a roundup of new poetry to read this November, with the wonderful title "Glass Skulls, Luminosity, Soup, and Other Miracles". It is led by Malgorzata Lebda's collection Mer de Glace, in Mira Rosenthal's translation. The title will ring a bell for anyone living in the Alps. The opening lines quoted in the piece are lyrical, and the roundup makes a point of mentioning the translator's notes as part of the appeal. For someone who thinks about how language travels from one tongue to another, that detail is worth noticing. A translator's notes can be a small essay on the choices behind every line, a way of seeing the poem being made twice.

Also from Literary Hub, there is a short, atmospheric passage titled "The Shared Life of Egan and Lucian". It is set on a bay at sunset, around a place called Shep's Island, and appears to be the opening of a longer piece. The text I have is thin, so I can't say what becomes of Egan and Lucian. But the prose is described as atmospheric, and an opening like that, with light on water and a named island, may be worth a few minutes if you like to be drawn in by setting before you know the story.

From poetry I'd like to move to voices and characters, which I know matter most to you. The first is a piece by Megan Nolan on Agnes Owens's novel A Working Mother, which Nolan presents as an ode to working-class Scotland. This is an appreciation rather than a straightforward review, so it's written from the heart of a reader who loves the book. What recommends it is the kind of voice it celebrates: a writer from outside the usual literary milieu, giving a mother's working life its full weight on the page. If you enjoy narrators and characters you can step into without any preparation, this seems a lovely way to meet an author you may not know.

Then there is Annie Proulx. The New York Times reviews Annie Proulx Stories, a career-spanning collection of her short fiction. The reviewer notes her dense, thorny prose, and that phrase is a good description of her style. Her sentences can feel like the landscapes she writes about, compressed and rough-edged, full of odd, exact words. Her characters are sharp too. A collection that gathers her work across a whole career is a good way to hear how that voice has developed, and to enjoy the music of it, which is unlike anything smooth or conventional.

On the radio, BBC Radio 4's Bookclub has an episode with Matt Haig, discussing The Midnight Library. You'll know the premise: Nora Seed finds herself in a library holding all the alternative lives she might have led. It's a narrator-led novel, with the reader inside Nora's head as she tries on different versions of herself. What Bookclub adds is the conversation between the author and a group of readers, so you hear how the book has landed with ordinary people, and what Haig says about it in return. It's a gentle listen, and a good one if you like hearing writers talk about their own characters.

For something that teaches culture and history from the inside, Literary Hub carries an essay called "The Ghostly and the Real: On Spirit Worlds in African Literature". It looks at how African writers treat the boundary between the living and the dead, where ancestors and spirits are not merely metaphors or decoration but part of lived reality. That is a different stance from the way Western fiction often handles ghosts, as something to be explained away or feared. For a reader who likes novels that let you into a world on its own terms, without a lecture, the essay should be a rewarding way of approaching a whole tradition. It could also open interesting questions about how a narrator's sense of reality shapes everything the reader accepts.

Now to the experimental end of the shelf. The Guardian reviews Tom McCarthy's new novel, The Rhyl Poster, and the headline asks whether this avant-garde spy drama is worth the riddles. The book follows a war-scarred jurist with a painkiller dependency through a hallucinatory crisis. The reviewer, it seems, finds the riddles frustrating. So this is not a straightforward recommendation, but a piece that sets out a real debate: whether McCarthy's method pays off, or whether the puzzle gets in the way of the story. If you enjoy thrillers, there's something intriguing in a spy story told through a mind that can't be trusted, and even a sceptical review can help you decide if you want to take it on.

Also on the subject of fiction and what it can do, the New Statesman has an interview with Missouri Williams, under the title "Fiction has its own kind of truth". I only have the headline, so I can't tell you what she actually says. But it's a phrase that sits well with the whole of this briefing, and it's one that anyone who teaches literature has probably wrestled with, the idea that an invented story can tell you something a factual account cannot. It may be worth looking up if the subject appeals.

Turning to music and history, the New York Times reviews Sound Tracks by Graeme Lawson. It tells a story of human music-making through ancient instruments, blending music, archaeology and history. I like the idea of the book very much. Rather than starting from scores or composers, it starts from objects, instruments made and played long before anyone wrote the music down, and it uses them to tell a story about people. Given your love of classical music and of history that comes alive, it seems a natural fit. It's the sort of book that makes you listen differently afterwards.

In the same spirit, Literary Hub has a list of ten great nonfiction titles to read in November. It includes new work by Hermione Lee and by Orlando Swain. One book singled out is Matt O'Hara's The Flying Death, about poison, plunder and the search for a medicine in the Amazon. That is a striking set of subjects to bring together, and it sounds like narrative nonfiction with a real sense of adventure and moral weight. I don't have more detail on the other titles, but a list from a source like this is a useful starting point if you're planning winter reading.

And to mark the calendar, Literary Hub's This Week in Literary History recalls that on the fifth of November, nineteen thirty, Sinclair Lewis received the Nobel Prize in Literature, honoured for his vivid description and wit. It's a short note, but there is something nice in the words chosen: vivid description and wit are still two good things to look for in any novel, and they might make a neat starting point for a class conversation about how writers are remembered, and what a prize actually praises.

Finally, there is the matter of the Booker Prize, which is still generating coverage. The Independent asks what it was like for this year's judges to read one hundred and sixty-three books in seven months. I only have the headline, so I can't tell you what the judges said about the experience. But the figure alone is wonderful to think about: more than twenty books a month, every month, for most of a year, and all of them to be weighed against one another. And News24 offers a guide to the unmissable titles in the running for the prize, though again what I have is a summary headline rather than the full list. Between the two, you have a sense of the effort behind the award and a pointer to where to look for the shortlist-stage novels, should you want to know what the fuss is about.

So, a morning of ecstatic verse, thorny sentences and spirits at the table. May whatever you pick up next be as good company as Nora Seed, and a good deal more cheerful than a jurist in a hallucinatory crisis.

around.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Monday the second of November, and the days ahead around Grenoble and the Grésivaudan are rich in talks, concerts and a few long-running exhibitions to keep in mind.

Let me start with what's closest. This afternoon, at half past two, there's a free guided visit of the Saint-Laurent archaeological museum in Grenoble. It's a chance to see the city's buried past up close, and since it costs nothing, it could fit neatly into a quiet Monday. Tomorrow evening, the third of November, the film club at Le Belvédère in Saint-Martin-d'Uriage shows Sidney Lumet's The Verdict at half past eight. It's a courtroom drama built around a memorable central character, so it sits close to the kind of fiction you enjoy. On Wednesday the fourth, Le Dauphiné Libéré announces a new writing and creative workshop in Allevard, led by Véronique Buthod. The details are thin, so I can't say much about the format, but given your love of writing, it may be worth a phone call to find out more.

The MC2 in Grenoble has a busy few days from Thursday. On the fifth of November, there's a preliminary talk with Marion Grange on the memory of the transatlantic slave trade. It's a serious subject, and a rich one if you like to see history approached through culture. The same evening, and again on the sixth, the MC2 stages Foutue bergerie, a production directed by Pierre Guillois. The listing doesn't say what the play is about, so I can only point you to the name. For something with a child, the MC2 also offers Petite Dolto, a family theatre show by Elsa Imbert, suitable for ages eight and up, on the fifth and sixth as well.

Meylan has its own offering for younger audiences. On Friday the sixth of November at ten in the morning, Hexagone Scène nationale presents T·R·U·C, from the company En Cie d'Eux. It's an object-theatre piece that mixes theatre, music and dance, for children aged five and up, and it lasts fifty minutes. There are three more dates listed if Friday morning doesn't suit. Then on the tenth of November at eight in the evening, Hexagone hosts Faire troupeau, by the company Frag. It's in French and blends theatre with documentary, and the programme describes it as a joyful odyssey about the power of the collective. It runs for an hour and twenty minutes, and may interest you both as a language experience and as a piece of storytelling.

Turning to music, there are two things to note. On Sunday the eighth of November, Vizille hosts a concert pairing organ and violin, as reported by Le Dauphiné Libéré. The announcement is brief, with no programme or time in the text, so it's worth checking before you go, but organ and violin together is a lovely combination for an autumn Sunday. The other is a concert of sixteenth and seventeenth-century polyphony at the Salle Olivier Messiaen in Grenoble. The listing on jds.fr has seat and booking information, but the date isn't given in the text I have, so do check the listing before planning around it. Early vocal music in that hall could be a real treat.

Now for the exhibitions, which give you more flexibility. In Grenoble, Anne Truitt. Libérer la couleur is free and runs until the tenth of January. It's a show about painting and colour, the sort that invites you to think about how visual art and language speak to each other. Also in Grenoble, Encordés, dans les pas des guides pionniers, runs until the twenty-seventh of February, following the pioneering mountain guides. The listing is short, but it ties in nicely with the Belledonne landscape you live in. And in Allevard, there's a free temporary exhibition called L'avant de l'après, which stays open until the thirty-first of October next year. There's no detail beyond the title, but with that much time you can pick any weekend and make an outing of it, perhaps combined with the writing workshop if you go on the fourth.

There's one more to keep in mind. Yesterday, the Maison Bergès museum in Villard-Bonnot ran a guided visit called La force de l'eau, la force de l'art, linking the history of hydroelectric power with art. It's listed as a regular visit, so it may well come round again. I'd check the museum's calendar for the next date. Yesterday morning also saw the farmers' market at Saint-Martin-d'Uriage, from nine to half past twelve. That one has passed, but I mention it in case you're looking for a regular market rhythm in the area.

To sum up the week: the archaeological museum today, a courtroom classic tomorrow, then a lively run of theatre and talks at the MC2 and in Meylan, with organ and violin on Sunday to close it off. Enjoy the week, Yamuna, and may it hold at least one good story.
around.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Monday the second of November, and the week ahead in and around Grenoble is quietly rich in history, music, theatre and a few exhibitions that will stay open long after this week is over.

Let me begin with the one thing that happens today, and it belongs to the history-minded side of your tastes. This afternoon, Monday the second of November, at half past two, there is a free guided visit of the Saint-Laurent archaeological museum in Grenoble. The listing, from Isère Attractivité, offers it as a chance to see the city's buried past up close. If your afternoon is free, it is a gentle way to spend an hour or so, and an easy one, since it costs nothing and sits right in the city. If you can't manage today, it is still worth knowing the museum is there, ready for a quieter day.

That leads naturally to the other history item of the week, which is rather more serious in tone. On Thursday the fifth of November, at the MC2 in Grenoble, there is a preliminary talk with Marion Grange, built around the memory of the transatlantic slave trade. The MC2 calls it a préambule, an introduction that sets the ground before a larger programme. The listing gives no more than that, so I can't tell you what it precedes or how long it lasts. But for someone who believes that stories can teach history better than essays do, it is a thoughtful subject, and one that you may find useful when you think of what novels have done to keep that memory alive. It would be worth a quick look at the MC2 page for the time and for what follows the talk.

Staying with the past, but in a different register, there is the Maison Bergès, the Museum of the Houille blanche, in Villard-Bonnot. It held a guided visit on Sunday the first of November, called "La force de l'eau, la force de l'art", linking the history of hydroelectric power with art. That one has already passed, I'm afraid, but the title says it is a regular guided visit, so it may well come round again. The Grésivaudan agenda is where to check. It is a nice pairing, water and power set beside art, and it speaks to the valley you actually live above. This is the landscape where industry and beauty have long sat side by side.

Now for words and stories. On Wednesday the fourth of November, in Allevard, Le Dauphiné Libéré announces a new writing and creative workshop led by Véronique Buthod. I'm sorry to say the text gives no further details, neither the time nor the venue, nor whether it is for beginners or for seasoned writers. But a new writing workshop in Allevard, on a day in the middle of the week, may be of interest to someone who spends her days with language. A short call or a look at the paper's page would settle the practical questions. It is also quite close to home, which always helps in November, when the evenings draw in.

The following evening has a story of another sort. On Tuesday the third of November, at half past eight, the film club at Le Belvédère, the Jeannine Creissels cultural centre in Saint-Martin-d'Uriage, shows Sidney Lumet's The Verdict. Le Grésivaudan lists it in its agenda. It is a courtroom drama, and a strong one, built around a memorable central character, which is exactly the sort of thing that draws you in when it comes to fiction. Whether you've seen it before or not, a film club screening has a particular pleasure: the room goes quiet, and everyone follows the same story together. It is tomorrow evening, so if you want to go, you have a little planning to do today.

On to music, where there are two things to tell you. First, on Sunday the eighth of November in Vizille, Le Dauphiné Libéré announces a concert pairing organ and violin. The text is brief, so I can't tell you the programme, the church, or the time. But the combination of those two instruments is a lovely one, the organ's breadth set against the violin's single voice, and Vizille is not far from Grenoble. A Sunday classical concert is a good way to close a week, and it would be worth finding the details before the weekend.

The second is a concert of sixteenth- and seventeenth-century polyphony at the Salle Olivier Messiaen in Grenoble. The jds.fr site gives seats, tickets and booking information, but the text I have does not give the date, so please check the listing before you plan anything. Polyphony of that period has a beautiful, interwoven quality, voices following and answering one another, and if you enjoy music as language, I think it may appeal. It is the kind of concert where a hall like that one, named for Messiaen, feels like the right place to hear it.

Let me turn now to the exhibitions, which have the advantage that you needn't hurry. In Grenoble, "Anne Truitt. Libérer la couleur" runs from the third of October 2026 until the tenth of January 2027, and it is free. It is a show about painting and colour, and I'll be honest that I have little more detail than that. But a title like "freeing colour" suggests something to stand in front of slowly, and I know you enjoy the way paintings and written works speak to one another. You might go with a particular passage of prose in your head, and see whether the colours answer it. With more than two months to run, it asks nothing of you this week.

Also in Grenoble is "Encordés, dans les pas des guides pionniers", which runs from the fifteenth of October 2026 to the twenty-seventh of February 2027. It follows the pioneering mountain guides, and the text is short, so I can only say that it takes you into the history of the people who first led others up the peaks. From your home in Les Adrets, with Belledonne above you, the subject is close. There is something fitting about learning how those early guides worked, roped together, when you can look up and see the mountains they were facing. It also runs well into the winter, so it could suit a snowy afternoon when walking is less appealing.

And in Allevard, there is a free temporary exhibition called "L'avant de l'après", open until the thirty-first of October 2027. That is nearly a year from now, which makes it a long-running local show. The listing gives no further detail, so I can't say what it is about. But it is free, it's in Allevard, and with that much time left, it is the kind of place you might drop into on a weekend when you're out that way, perhaps alongside the writing workshop if the timing suits.

Now for the stage, where the MC2 and the Hexagone in Meylan have a busy few days. At the MC2 in Grenoble, on the fifth and sixth of November, there is "Foutue bergerie", a theatre production directed by Pierre Guillois. The listing gives nothing about the play itself, so I'll simply tell you the dates and the director, and leave the curiosity to you. Also at the MC2 is "Petite Dolto", a family theatre show by Elsa Imbert, suitable for ages eight and up. The listing gives the fifth and sixth of November, though the weekdays given for it don't quite match the other listings, so the dates are the safe thing to go by. If you have a child, or a young relation, or a pupil's younger sibling who might enjoy an outing, it sounds like a pleasant one.

At the Hexagone, the national stage in Meylan, there are two more. On Friday the sixth of November at ten in the morning, En Cie d'Eux presents "T·R·U·C", an object-theatre show that mixes theatre, music and dance, for children aged five and up. It lasts fifty minutes, and there are three more dates listed, so there is room to choose. A morning start means it is clearly aimed at younger audiences, perhaps school groups and families. It is a gentle option, and Meylan is close to home.

For adults, on Tuesday the tenth of November at eight in the evening, also at the Hexagone, the company Frag presents "Faire troupeau". It is in French, a blend of theatre and documentary, and the text describes it as a joyful odyssey about the power of the collective. It runs one hour twenty. I like the idea of documentary and theatre meeting, since it suggests real voices and real stories shaped for the stage. For a teacher, there is perhaps something of the classroom in it too, the way a group becomes more than the sum of its members, though that is my own thought, not the listing's.

Finally, a word about the weekend just gone, since you may have missed it. On Sunday the first of November, from nine until half past twelve, there was a farmers' market at Saint-Martin-d'Uriage, a good morning out for local produce close to Grenoble. It has passed, but it is a reminder that the little village markets carry on through the autumn, and that the Grésivaudan agenda is worth glancing at when you fancy a Sunday morning outing.

If I were to sketch the week for you, it might go like this. Today, if you have the afternoon, the archaeological museum in Grenoble. Tomorrow evening, The Verdict at Saint-Martin-d'Uriage. Wednesday, the writing workshop in Allevard, if it suits. Thursday, the talk on memory at the MC2. Then, with more time, the Vizille concert on Sunday and the Meylan evening on the tenth. The exhibitions, the colour of Anne Truitt, the mountain guides, and Allevard's long-running show, can wait for whenever you have a free hour.

I hope the week treats you kindly, Yamuna, and that something here sends you out into the autumn light.

bfi.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Monday the second of November, and the last two days have brought a lot of theatre news for your programme, with Hamlet and Orwell's 1984 at the centre of it.

Let me start with Hamlet, since he's on the session 2027 list and is turning up in several guises at once. The most intriguing item is from Planet Hugill, which reviews Chelsea Opera Group's performance of Ambroise Thomas's opera Hamlet. Jacques Imbrailo sings the prince and Haegee Lee is Ophélie, with Jonathon Cole-Swinard in charge. The review's headline says "Forget Shakespeare", which is cheeky, and it argues that the opera makes a strong case for itself and is led with real sympathy. I only have the headline and the outline of the review, so I can't tell you how the librettists reshaped the story. But the idea is a lovely one for a Hamlet class. Any adaptation has to choose what to keep and what to cut, and those choices tell you what the adapters thought the play was about. With première students, you could ask what an opera needs from this story that a play doesn't, and what is lost when it is sung. And since you enjoy classical music, the Ophélie spelling alone might tempt you to listen to a recording.

Then there is the more contemporary Hamlet. Matinee Musicals reports that Radiohead's Hamlet, Hail to the Thief, begins its London run at the Barbican. Broadway Shows, in its roundup of London theatre for November, also lists a Radiohead-scored Hamlet, alongside a production of Nero and a Sondheim celebration. Both pieces are headline-only, so I can't say how the album and the play are put together. But the pairing is surely worth a few minutes in class. You could ask students what music does to a soliloquy, and whether a score can say something about Hamlet's state of mind that words alone can't. Even without seeing the production, the very idea of setting a Shakespearean tragedy to a modern band's work invites a good discussion about whether the play belongs to its own time or to every time.

The third Hamlet is a casting story. The London Evening Standard profiles Sam Blenkin and his new West End role as Hamlet, after earlier work that includes Harry Potter. Your students will probably know him, or at least know that world, and there's something engaging about a young actor moving from a modern phenomenon to the most famous part in English drama. It could open a conversation about who gets to play Hamlet, and how an actor's earlier roles shape the way an audience first meets him. It's a small thing, but it might bring the play closer to students who think of Shakespeare as remote.

Staying with Shakespeare in performance, Plays International reviews a new Arden study, Shakespeare in the Theatre: Phyllida Lloyd, by Elizabeth Schafer and David Bullen. It looks at the director's work on Shakespeare, and it should be useful for both Twelfth Night and Hamlet on the 2027 list. I haven't got the details of which productions the book covers, so I can't promise specifics. But the Arden series is a trusted name, and the book seems designed to show how a director reads a play and makes choices that an audience then experiences as simply "the play". If you're looking for a way to lead students from the text to the stage, a director's decisions about a single scene, such as how to stage Viola's first entrance in Twelfth Night, make a good exercise, and a book like this might supply a few ideas.

Two lighter Shakespeare notes. UPI's "On This Day" column marks the date Othello debuted in England. Again, I only have the headline, but it's a nice little hook for a lesson opening, a reminder that these plays were once brand-new entertainment. And The Guardian marks thirty years of Baz Luhrmann's Romeo + Juliet, with a feature on how it made teenagers fall in love with Shakespeare. I know cinema news isn't usually your priority, but the angle here is a teaching one. It asks what actually brings young readers to Shakespeare, and whether a bold, noisy, modern reworking is a betrayal of the text or a doorway into it. For seconde students, that could make a good opening debate before you ever open the book.

Now to 1984, which is on your oral themes list and has been busy this weekend. Two reviews of the production at the Royal Lyceum in Edinburgh have appeared. Everything Theatre has a review, and Fife Today gives it four stars, calling it a challenging watch and a powerful recreation of Orwell's novel. Neither of those gives me enough to say how the production handles, say, Room 101 or the telescreens, but the verdict is clear, and "challenging" is a useful word. It suggests the staging doesn't let the audience off lightly, which is rather the point of the book. If any of your students happen to have a theatre trip in Britain planned, or if you want to look for reviews and production photographs to show in class, this is a good production to look up. You could ask students how a novel that takes place so much inside one man's head can work on a stage, where the audience sees bodies, not thoughts.

On a more heartening note, the Belleville News-Democrat reports that students at Rock Valley College have staged 1984. The report is brief, but I like the idea of young people tackling this particular book, since it is so much about what happens when people lose the freedom to speak and think for themselves. If your terminale students were ever to try something similar, even a few scenes read aloud, it might do more than an essay to help them feel the weight of the language, especially Newspeak.

There's a natural companion to this in the theatre news as well. Plays International writes about The Lives of Others at the Adelphi Theatre, the stage version of the film about surveillance in East Germany. The parallel with 1984 is obvious, since both are about a state that listens, watches and records. But the contrast is interesting too. Orwell invented his world, while this story comes from a real one, where people really were watched. For a class discussion of state surveillance, you could set the two side by side, one imagined, one historical, and ask which unsettles students more, and why. It also speaks to your love of novels and stories that teach history better than history essays do, since a stage piece like this lets students step into a place they've never known.

Related to that, and still on the theme of why we tell these stories, blue News has an interview with the filmmaker Raoul Peck, who says that "art without a purpose is not art". The piece is short, but the line is a good provocation, and it touches on documentary and artistic commitment, which I think you'd enjoy. It would work as a starting question for older students. Does a novel like 1984 or The Handmaid's Tale have a purpose, and does that make it better or worse as art? Some students will say a story shouldn't preach. Others will say that the greatest stories always have something to say. It might even work as a prompt for the written commentary exercises that the BFI favours.

That brings me to Margaret Atwood. The Peterborough Examiner has an opinion piece, prompted by her memoir covering five decades of writing, which weighs which of her works still matter. I only have the headline, so I can't tell you which books the writer picks. But it's a good prompt for the oral list, where The Handmaid's Tale sits. A student preparing for the oral might ask, "Why does this book still matter?", and that is often the question examiners are really asking. You could even turn the opinion piece's premise into an exercise, asking students to make their own case, in two minutes, for why a particular novel from the list deserves to last.

Now a note on Dickens, for Great Expectations on the 2027 programme. The Times of India has a piece about a London house that Charles Dickens once rented for eighty pounds a year, and about a three-point-two million pound restoration that removed later alterations. The detail that appeals to me is the idea of peeling away later layers to get back to something closer to the author's own time. That's something literary study does too, in a way, since we're always trying to read past our own assumptions to the world the book came from. For Great Expectations, where houses and rooms carry so much meaning, think of Satis House or Wemmick's little castle. It might help students to see how much a writer's surroundings shaped what he wrote. I don't have the name of the house from the headline, so it would be worth checking the full article if you'd like to use it, perhaps with a photograph on the board.

Finally, something for your own reading pleasure, with a possible link to the programme. Collider has ranked what it calls the ten best spy novels of all time. I only have the title, so I can't say what's on the list, or whether Conrad's The Secret Agent, from the 2027 list, appears. The format is a generic ranking, but a ranked list is a good thing to argue with. Students could be asked to write their own top three, or to explain why Conrad's novel, with its anarchists, its London streets and its bleak irony, belongs in the conversation, or doesn't. Since you enjoy thrillers, you might also simply find a new book to read by the fire this evening.

So that's the picture: plenty of Hamlet on stage and in song, Orwell proving as unsettling as ever, and a few small ideas to carry into the classroom this week. Enjoy the November light over the Grésivaudan, Yamuna.

Good morning, Yamuna. Here is a gentle gathering of good news from the last two days, with a fair few stories of language, music and small kindnesses.

Let me begin with nature, where the news is wonderfully concrete. On Corvo, a small island in the Azores, the public lights are switched off for the last five nights of October. The reason is that young seabird fledglings, on their first flight towards the sea, can be confused by artificial light. With the island in darkness, they find their way. Good News Network reports that thirty thousand birds have already been saved this way, which is a lovely example of a whole community changing its habits for the sake of creatures that cannot ask. In a similar spirit, Upworthy tells of a Caribbean island that had come to look like a moonscape after goats and rats were introduced. Both have now been removed, the island is flourishing again, and the coral reefs offshore have recovered too. The piece is brief, but the lesson is clear: sometimes recovery begins with taking away what should never have arrived. And on the practical side, The Optimist Daily reports that California's governor has signed a bill legalising plug-in balcony solar panels. Renters can use them without owning a roof, hiring a contractor or paying large sums upfront, so clean energy becomes something an ordinary flat-dweller can reach.

Now to words, writing and music, which I suspect you will enjoy. ARTE has a documentary called "À la recherche de l'écriture oubliée", in which the archaeologist François Desset describes how, after fifteen years of research, he deciphered Elamite linear script. It is a writing system from southern Iran, more than four thousand years old, long thought unreadable. It is a real piece of linguistic detective work, and you can watch it until April next year. From the Times of India comes a story that might delight your seconde and première classes: a London house that Charles Dickens once rented for eighty pounds a year has been through a restoration costing three point two million pounds, which removed later alterations. It is a nice thought, a physical place where the author once lived, being carefully returned to something closer to his time. And in classical music, The Guardian reports that Sofia Demetriades, a teenage violinist, has won BBC Young Musician 2026, in the competition's first all-female final. The judges praised her performance of the Tchaikovsky Violin Concerto for its insight and poetry, which is a rather fine thing to be said of anyone at that age.

Music also turns up in a much quieter setting. Upworthy shares a moment from a senior home, where an eighty-five-year-old woman sang a cover of Fleetwood Mac's "Landslide" and moved the whole room. There is something about that song, and about a voice that has lived a long while, that I imagine made the silence afterwards very full. Staying with later life, Good News Network brings us Barbara Thompson and Fred Jenkins, who are both widowed and have fallen in love at eighty-eight. They met at the gym, after Barbara moved to Oscott Retirement Village in Birmingham. It is a tender story, and a reminder that new chapters do not keep to any timetable.

Next, a handful of stories about everyday kindness. Closer to home, franceinfo has a portrait from Grenoble, published on the first of November for Toussaint. Sébastien Roca, a cemetery keeper, describes how families who come to honour their dead confide in him and tell him their stories. He says he feels useful to others, and it is a humane reminder that comfort often comes from people in unexpected jobs. In Florida, Good News Network reports on two teachers, Maren and David Douglass, who found a schoolgirl sitting in the dirt at a bus stop at the end of their driveway. They surprised her with a bench. The kindness went viral, and the video shows her doing a little jig of delight. Another story, also from Good News Network, is about a deaf woman whose support dog woke her in the night, insisting that something was wrong. Her husband had fallen down the stairs and was left bleeding and unconscious, and she credits the dog's quick action with saving his life. And Positive News describes a new series of all-female fight nights, raising money for free boxing classes that help women rebuild their confidence after abusive relationships. The article is short, but the project is practical, and its purpose is clear.

There is also a gentler note about family life. The Optimist Daily reports that Italy's federation of paediatricians has designed a box of games to help parents talk with their children at dinner. According to the headline, restaurants in Sardinia are now banning phones at family meals. It is a small idea, but I like the picture of a table where conversation gets the first word.

Finally, two stories about learning and care. Upworthy reports on a large randomised experiment in which older students spent about eight minutes giving advice to younger pupils, and their own grades improved as a result. It is a short piece, but a hopeful finding for anyone who believes that helping others helps us learn. And franceinfo reports that from this Monday, around three thousand "docteurs juniors" begin their final year of training out in the field. They work with growing autonomy in practices and health centres, mainly in areas short of general practitioners. It is a hopeful step against France's medical deserts, with, as one headline puts it, waiting times a little shorter.

That is all for this morning, Yamuna, and I hope the day treats you as kindly as a bench at the end of a driveway.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Monday the second of November, and the last couple of days have brought a pleasing mix of old scripts, sleeping birds and kindness in unexpected places.

Let me begin with the words and the music, which I suspect are closest to your heart. ARTE has a documentary called "À la recherche de l'écriture oubliée", in which the archaeologist François Desset describes how he deciphered Elamite linear script. This is a writing system from southern Iran, more than four thousand years old, and it had long been thought unreadable. It took him fifteen years of research. What I like about it is that it's a piece of pure detective work with language, patient, stubborn and slow, and the reward at the end is that voices from four millennia ago can be heard again. It's on ARTE's platform until April next year, so there's no rush, but it might be a lovely thing to save for an evening when the house is quiet. And if you ever want a way of showing seconde students what it means to read, in the deepest sense, it could be a charming starting point.

Staying with writing, but moving to London. The Times of India has a piece about a house that Charles Dickens once rented for eighty pounds a year. It has now been through a restoration costing three point two million pounds, which removed the later alterations and, presumably, let the house breathe more like the one he knew. It's a small story, but there's something moving about the idea of stripping away the layers that later generations added, so that a place can speak more clearly of the writer who lived there. If any of your students are reading Dickens, or are about to, it gives them a real address to hold on to, a physical room where a narrator's voice was once at work.

And on the musical side, The Guardian reports that Sofia Demetriades, a teenage violinist, has won BBC Young Musician twenty twenty-six, in the competition's first all-female final. The judges praised her performance of the Tchaikovsky Violin Concerto for its insight and poetry, which are exactly the words one hopes to hear about that piece. The broadcast is on the BBC, so perhaps not somewhere you usually look, but it's a warm piece of news from the classical world, and a milestone for the competition as well.

Staying with music, but at a very different scale, Upworthy has a short, sweet story about an eighty-five-year-old woman in a senior home who performed a cover of Fleetwood Mac's "Landslide", and moved the whole room. There's nothing grand about the setting, and that's rather the point. A song about time passing and about growing older, sung by someone who knows what that means, tends to carry a weight no stage lighting can add. It's the sort of concert moment you'd probably enjoy most, the kind where the room goes quiet because everyone is listening.

From music to the natural world, where there are two encouraging stories this morning. The first is from Corvo, a small island in the Azores. For the last five nights of October, the public lighting on the island is switched off, so that young seabirds, the fledglings, can find their way to the sea. Artificial light can confuse them on their first flights, and so the community simply turns the lights off. Good News Network reports that thirty thousand birds have already been saved. I find it lovely because it's so concrete. There's no grand programme, just a village deciding that a few dark nights are a fair price for a few thousand lives, and then doing it, year after year.

The second comes from the Caribbean, via Upworthy. An island there had become so barren after goats and rats were introduced that it looked like a moonscape. Both animals have now been removed, and the island is flourishing again. The coral reefs offshore have recovered too. The article is brief, so I can't tell you more about which island it is or how the work was done, but the shape of the story is clear and satisfying. Take away what should never have been there, and the land and the sea start to mend themselves. It's a nice companion to the Corvo story, both being about people deciding to step back, or to put right something they had done.

Now to the quieter, human stories, which this morning are especially tender. Let me start close to home. Franceinfo has a portrait, from the first of November, so Toussaint, of Sébastien Roca, a cemetery keeper in Grenoble. He describes how families come to honour their dead and, as he puts it, confide in him and tell him their stories. He says he feels useful to others. It's a gentle reminder of how much comfort can come from simply being the person who listens, in a place where people most need someone to. For a literature teacher, there's something quietly novelistic about it: a man in a cemetery who becomes, without quite meaning to, the keeper of everybody's stories.

On a lighter note, but still about love and companionship later in life, Good News Network tells of Barbara Thompson and Fred Jenkins, both widowed, who have fallen in love again at eighty-eight. They met at the gym, after Barbara moved to Oscott Retirement Village in Birmingham. I would happily read a novel that began with that meeting. It's a happy ending that arrives late and sits all the more sweetly for it.

Good News Network also has a dramatic one. A deaf woman says her support dog woke her in the night and insisted that something was wrong. Her husband had fallen down the stairs, and was lying bleeding and unconscious. Because the dog got her out of bed, she was able to get help. It's a story of an animal's quick thinking, and of the particular kind of attention that a support dog gives. Nobody could have asked for a better narrator of that night than a dog who simply would not be ignored.

And from Florida, another Good News Network story, with a teaching connection. Maren and David Douglass, who are both teachers, found a schoolgirl sitting in the dirt at a bus stop at the end of their driveway. So they gave her a surprise: a bench. The kindness went viral, and the video shows her delight, which, I'm told, includes a little jig. It's such a small thing, a bench, and it's exactly the kind of thing that a teacher notices. The girl had been waiting there every day, and someone saw it and did something simple about it.

Next, two stories about schools and health, which both suggest that sensible ideas can have an outsized effect. The first comes via Upworthy and describes a large randomised experiment. Older students spent about eight minutes giving advice to younger pupils, and their own grades improved. The article is short, so I don't have the details of the age groups or the size of the improvement. But the finding is a hopeful one for anyone who believes that explaining something, or encouraging someone else, helps you to understand and believe in it yourself. You'll recognise this from any classroom. Everyone who has taught knows that the best way to learn a poem is to try to explain it to someone else.

The second is from franceinfo, and it concerns the health system. From today, around three thousand "docteurs juniors" are beginning their final year of training out in the field, working in practices and health centres with growing autonomy. They are going mainly to areas that are short of GPs, which is to say, to the places affected by what we call the déserts médicaux. The title of the piece quotes someone saying that waiting times should be "un peu moins longs", a little shorter, which is a modest promise, but a real one. It's a hopeful step for rural areas, and for places like our own mountains, where a doctor's appointment can sometimes feel like a long journey.

Finally, three stories about practical community ideas, each pointing towards something a little better in everyday life.

Positive News describes a new series of all-female fight nights. They aim to raise money for free boxing classes, which help women rebuild their confidence after abusive relationships. The piece is short, but the project is concrete and has a clear purpose. A fight night, with its drama and its crowd, turns into a means of funding quiet, practical help, and I think there's something fitting in that. Strength, after all, can mean many things.

The Optimist Daily has two stories. In California, the governor has signed a bill legalising plug-in balcony solar panels. Renters can use them without a roof of their own, without a contractor and without large upfront costs. It's a practical idea, making clean energy available to people who rent, who have so often been left out of such schemes. Anyone with a balcony and a bit of sun might one day be able to join in, which I think is rather a nice thought.

The other is about family life. Italy's federation of paediatricians has designed a box of games to help parents talk with their children at dinner. The headline says that Sardinian restaurants are now banning phones for families at meals. I can only tell you what the headline says, but the intention is clear enough, and rather charming: to bring conversation back to the table, with a little help from some games. Whether or not it spreads, it's a kind thought to carry into the evening meal.

So there we are: a forgotten script read again, a village in the dark for the sake of the birds, and a bench at the end of a driveway, and I hope that something among them keeps you company on your walk down into the valley today.

They will work in practices and health centres with growing autonomy, and they are going mainly to areas that are short of general practitioners. It is a response to what the French call medical deserts, the towns and villages where finding a doctor can be a real struggle. One of the voices quoted says to expect "slightly shorter waiting times", which is a modest promise but a welcome one. It is not a miracle cure, but it is a practical step, and in the countryside it may matter a great deal.

Professor Yves Martinet, quoted by franceinfo, says that stopping smoking for a month multiplies by five your chances of quitting for good. It is a simple message, and he delivers it in an encouraging way. If someone you know has been thinking about stopping, this might be a kind moment to mention it.

Since yesterday was the first of November, there are a couple of stories that belong to the days of remembrance, and I rather liked both of them. The first is from right on your doorstep. Franceinfo has a portrait from Grenoble of a cemetery keeper named Sébastien Roca. For Toussaint, when families come to honour their dead, he describes how he comforts people who are grieving. He says, and I'll translate, that families confide in him and tell him their stories, and that this makes him feel useful to others. It is a small, humane piece, and it made me think of how many characters in fiction are exactly like this: the quiet figure at the edge of the scene who sees everything and says very little. I suspect you'd find in him the beginnings of a narrator.

The second story is from Tarbes, in the south-west. Franceinfo reports that the town council has voted a social tariff for abandoned graves and plots, so that families on modest incomes can afford them. Good morning, Yamuna. It's a thoughtful couple of days for watching and listening, with a lot of Arte to savour, some lovely music, and a few thrillers to keep you company as the evenings draw in.

Let me start with Arte, where there is plenty of history told as a story. The one I'd put first is a film called "À la recherche de l'écriture oubliée". The archaeologist François Desset explains how, after fifteen years of research, he deciphered Elamite linear script, a writing system from southern Iran that is more than four thousand years old and was long thought unreadable. It is linguistic detective work, and for someone who spends her days with words it has a particular romance: a language coming back to life after four millennia. It is available until April twenty twenty-seven, so there's no rush.

Also on Arte is a documentary about the Afro-Turks, the descendants of people brought from East Africa to the Ottoman Empire from the sixteenth century onwards, most of whom live along the Aegean coast. It follows a history that has been marginalised for a very long time and is only now coming to light. It is in French, and it teaches through lived experience rather than through a textbook. Another Arte documentary asks whether Christianity really took away the pleasure of the ancient world. It draws on recent historical scholarship, including Diarmaid MacCulloch's book on sex and Christianity, and it stays up until the twenty-seventh of November, twenty thirty-one. History that reads like a story, as you like it.

Two more from Arte are gentler. One is an animated essay called "Et si le vide n'existait pas ?", which follows more than two thousand years of thinking about the void, from cosmology to packaging and the fountains of Florence, drawing on Lipovetsky's "L'ère du vide". It's erudite but accessible. The other is a documentary called "Qu'est-ce qu'on va faire de toi ?", set in a socially mixed class of five-year-olds at a priority education school in Paris's eleventh arrondissement. It catches how small children see the world, with humour and tenderness, and it is available until April twenty twenty-seven. As a teacher, you may find it touching.

Now to music and dance. The Royal Ballet and Opera has put out a short video of Sae Maeda dancing the Dance of the Mirlitons from The Nutcracker, as a little Christmas teaser. It's light and festive, a pleasant way to begin November with ballet, and it's on their YouTube channel. The same channel has a video of Julia Bullock and Jakub Józef Orliński singing from Handel's Theodora at The Royal Opera. It's Katie Mitchell's production, conducted by Harry Bicket, and the staging gives the story a feminist reading, which makes it more than a simple concert excerpt.

On the recording side, The Guardian reviews Vasily Petrenko and the Royal Philharmonic's new recording of Strauss's Alpine Symphony on Harmonia Mundi. The reviewer finds it expansive and vivid, with a mystic vision guiding Petrenko through this monumental work, and compares it with two other recent recordings. If you like music that paints a landscape, and you live in the mountains, it might be one to hear. And there is some good news from the BBC. Sofia Demetriades, a teenage violinist, has won BBC Young Musician twenty twenty-six, in the competition's first all-female final. The judges praised her Tchaikovsky Violin Concerto for its insight and poetry. That's on the BBC, not one of your usual platforms, but it's a warm story all the same.

For theatre, The Guardian's round-up of the best theatre to stream this month leads with Milo Rau's four-hour documentary play about the Gisèle Pelicot trial. The Young Vic is staging it at County Hall in London on the thirtieth of November, though it has sold out. The paper quotes a response that it "just floors you". The same round-up also points to a stream of Tom Stoppard's Arcadia and to ecstatic dance in a Norwegian museum. Arcadia is a play that moves between centuries, so it may interest you for the classroom as well.

Finally, the series. On Netflix, MovieWeb is calling a detective thriller with four seasons the best since True Detective. The piece as I have it doesn't name the show, so I can't tell you which it is, but it may be worth a search, given how much you enjoy strong characters in a thriller. The Sydney Morning Herald's weekly streaming picks are led by Stephen Graham's serial killer thriller, with five other suggestions. The excerpt is brief and doesn't name the platform, so check before you plan an evening around it. If you'd like to see what else is coming, Time Out has a guide to seventeen films and shows new on Netflix this November, though it is quite general. The New York Times has a similar round-up covering HBO Max, Hulu, Apple TV and others, and the text I have is only the title, so I can't tell you what it recommends.

On HBO Max, there's a review of an episode of The Gilded Age in which the characters go dancing at a real club that would later host REM, Sting and Tina Turner. It's a nice touch of history woven through the fiction, and it should suit your taste for period drama.

That's the lot, and I hope something here earns a cosy evening by the fire.

Good morning, Yamuna, and happy Monday. It's the second of November, and I've gathered a few things for you: some good news, a little local culture, plenty to read and listen to, and a couple of notes for the classroom.

Let me begin on a small Atlantic island. On Corvo, in the Azores, the public lighting is switched off for the last five nights of October. The reason is that young seabirds, fledglings leaving their nests for the first time, are confused by artificial light and can lose their way to the sea. Good News Network reports that thirty thousand birds have already been saved this way. It's a lovely example of a whole community deciding that the dark is worth protecting. Closer to the human scale, Positive News describes a new series of all-female boxing nights. They raise money for free classes that help women rebuild their confidence after abusive relationships. The piece is short, but the purpose is clear and concrete.

Now closer to home. In Grenoble, there's a free exhibition called Anne Truitt, Libérer la couleur, running until the tenth of January. It's a show about painting and colour, and it should be a good one for a reader who likes to let a canvas drift towards a page of prose. Tomorrow evening, the third, at half past eight, the film club at Le Belvédère in Saint-Martin-d'Uriage shows Sidney Lumet's The Verdict. It's a courtroom drama built around a memorable, flawed central figure, which I suspect is just your sort of story. And on the eighth of November, in Vizille, Le Dauphiné Libéré announces a concert for organ and violin. The details are thin, but it's a classical evening not far from your door.

If you're looking further afield for art, Le Petit Bulletin in Lyon has put together ten exhibitions to see in November, under the lovely title "L'éloquence des choses muettes", the eloquence of silent things. I only have the headline, so I can't tell you what's in the ten, but the title alone suggests a gallery of objects that speak without words. And the National Gallery has a video in which Yinka Shonibare explains how Gainsborough's Mr and Mrs Andrews inspired his own work, Mr and Mrs Andrews without their Heads. He talks through his choices, and about class, power and identity. The two works are shown together for the first time, which makes it a rare chance to see a painting and its answer side by side.

On to books. At Literary Hub, Megan Nolan writes about Agnes Owens's novel A Working Mother, calling it an ode to working-class Scotland. It's an appreciation of a voice from outside the usual literary circles, and a reminder of how much a strong character can carry. In the New York Times, there's a review of a career-spanning collection, Annie Proulx Stories. The reviewer notes her dense, thorny prose, sentences that resist you a little before they reward you, and her sharp, unsentimental characters. If you like language with music in it, even rough music, she's worth a return visit. And on BBC Radio 4's Bookclub, Matt Haig talks with readers about The Midnight Library, in which Nora Seed moves through a library of alternative lives. It's a narrator-led novel, and the conversation should be good company for a walk or a drive down into the valley.

For music, there are two treats. The Royal Ballet and Opera has put online a performance by Julia Bullock and Jakub Józef Orliński from Handel's Theodora, in Katie Mitchell's production for The Royal Opera, conducted by Harry Bicket. The staging gives the story a feminist reading, and the two singers perform "To thee, thou glorious son of worth". And The Guardian reports that a teenage violinist, Sofia Demetriades, has won BBC Young Musician 2026, in the competition's first all-female final. The judges praised her Tchaikovsky Violin Concerto for its insight and poetry. It's a warm story, even if the broadcast itself is on the BBC.

Now a few notes for your terminale preparation. Planet Hugill reviews Chelsea Opera Group's performance of Ambroise Thomas's opera Hamlet, with Jacques Imbrailo as the prince and Haegee Lee as Ophélie, under Jonathon Cole-Swinard. The reviewer argues that the opera deserves attention alongside Shakespeare, and it could be an interesting way of showing pupils how the same story can be bent into another art form. And Everything Theatre reviews 1984 at the Royal Lyceum in Edinburgh. Since Orwell is on your oral-themes list, a review of how the novel behaves on stage may give you a few useful ideas about performance.

Finally, two items from France. Starting today, around three thousand "docteurs juniors" begin their final year of medical training out in the field, working with growing autonomy in practices and health centres. Franceinfo says they are mainly heading to areas short of GPs, and the hope is for slightly shorter waiting times. It's a modest but hopeful response to the problem of medical deserts. And, closer to your daily work, The Local France reports that high school blockades have restarted after the autumn holiday. Student leaders say the government's proposals do not go far enough. You may well hear about it from your seconde and première pupils this week.

That's everything for this morning, Yamuna. I hope your Monday is full of good sentences and good light, and that there's something lovely waiting for you at the end of it.
